When can a judge-free signal
grade reasoning?

Teacher-Forced Accuracy (TFA), tested by progressive generalization: within a family, across families, across datasets, and into agents, then flipped from ranking models to grading solutions.

17 models · 7 families · 8 datasets (math · olympiad · code) · 2 frontier judges · + rollout process value · + agentic
scroll or press → to advance
Motivation

The evaluation regress

In the agentic era a model produces a proof, plan, tool trajectory, or code patch. Exact-match is too brittle; an LLM judge adds another model whose reliability must itself be validated. To trust the judge you need human labels or an oracle, an evaluation regress.

Central question. When a gold reasoning trace exists, can a deterministic, judge-free signal do part of the job? TFA conditions the model on the gold prefix and asks whether it predicts each next token, local agreement with a trusted path. No judge, no rubric, one forward pass.

It might penalize valid alternate proofs, favor reference style, or under-score compressed and tool-using solutions. Those failure modes are measurable, which is exactly what makes it worth testing.

How we test it

Two questions, tested by progressive generalization

Q1 · can it rank models?

Compare mean TFA to accuracy (judge-free), then push it outward:

  1. within one model family (Qwen)
  2. across families
  3. across datasets (easy → hard)
  4. into agents

All against accuracy (judge-free); robustness to the choice of judge is in the appendix.

Q2 · can it grade one solution?

Then the harder test: does TFA tell a good solution from a bad one? We show it fails, prove why, and show everything we tried to fix it.

Then

A costlier signal that does grade (process rollout), and the path forward.

Q1 · step 1 · within a family

TFA tracks accuracy within the Qwen ladder

+0.6 to +1.0mean TFA vs accuracy, within Qwen
judge-freecompared to accuracy, not a judge

First, the purest test: does mean TFA order one family by accuracy (no judge involved)? Yes, and it is strongest on the hardest data, where weak models have the most room to separate.

It ranks the family by skill. Does that survive beyond Qwen?
Q1 · step 2 · beyond one family

It holds across families, on hard math

Add Mistral, Phi, OLMo, and math-specialized models. On hard math (Putnam, MATH) every family's size-ladder points up and to the right: a bigger, better model predicts the gold better, so it holds across families, not just Qwen. On easy, saturated data (GSM8K) some families invert: Phi's and OLMo's stronger models solve more but answer in a fuller, labeled style than the short, terse gold, so they predict it worse and the arrow points down. There the gold is so stylized that family style, not skill, drives the score.

Whether it holds or inverts depends on the data, which points straight to saturation, next.
Q1 · step 3 · beyond one dataset

Why it saturates on easy data and holds on hard

~0.03TFA range on GSM8K (easy)
~0.08TFA range on Putnam (hard)

The proof is saturation. On easy, near-ceiling data the whole ladder is squeezed into a tiny TFA band, so there is no room to separate models; on hard data the range widens. TFA's discriminating power is a direct function of how far the reference pushes models from ceiling.

So on saturated data a family style-offset can dominate, and the ranking can even invert.
Q1 · step 3 · the boundary

Strong on hard math, weak on code, negative on saturated GSM8K

+0.86Omni-MATH
+0.60Putnam
+0.43code
−0.37GSM8K

Pooling all families across all eight datasets gives one boundary map. It holds on hard, constrained references, weakens on code (many valid programs), and inverts on saturated grade-school math.

One rule: TFA ranks by quality only when the reference is a long, constrained trace and models share its style.
Q1 · step 3 · reconciliation

This reconciles the original TFA paper's 0.66

Putnam-AXIOM reported TFA-vs-accuracy at 0.66 (MATH) and 0.52 (Putnam), below our within-family +0.9 to +1.0. Not a disagreement: their numbers fall out once you match the metric (Kendall tau, the honest choice for a handful of models) and the model set, shown here across all four correlation measures.

All models = the full set including the math-specialized outliers (Qwen-Math, DeepSeek-Math, Mathstral), which reproduce the gold style beyond their solving skill and drag the pooled number down toward their 0.66 / 0.52. General families only = the general-purpose families (Qwen, Mistral, Phi, OLMo) with those outliers dropped, which recovers +0.86 / +0.88. Their headline 0.66 is simply our Kendall value on the full set.

Model-level reproduces exactly; their untested item-level claim (next) does not.
Q1 · step 4 · to agents

The whole boundary reaches coding agents

+1.00within Qwen-Coder (by scale)
+0.00across four coder families

On SWE-bench, teacher-forcing the human gold patch ranks one coder family's sizes by skill perfectly, but says nothing across families. CodeLlama reproduces the gold-patch style best while writing some of the worst code, the repository-patch version of the GSM8K offset.

Not “TFA works on agents,” but “the boundary does.”
Q2 · grading individual solutions

Now the harder question: can TFA grade one solution?

≈ 0MATH (per-item, beyond correctness)
+0.12GSM8K
+0.22Putnam

Controlling for correctness, the per-item TFA-vs-judge signal is zero on MATH, small on GSM8K, and only +0.22 on the hardest math. The small signals are real (they survive label-noise and contamination controls) but explain under 5% of variance, far too little to replace a judge.

Why a judge here, not accuracy? Grading a solution means scoring quality beyond right-or-wrong. Accuracy is binary and is exactly what we control for, and among the correct answers it has no variance at all, so ρ(TFA, accuracy | correct) is undefined. The item-level target has to be graded (a judge, or human grades). Model ranking (Q1) is the judge-free, accuracy-based half; robustness to the choice of judge is in the appendix.
A leaderboard, not a grader. Why?
Q2 · why, with proof

Because per-item TFA is 89-96% reference nuisance

89-96%reference nuisance
4-11%left for competence

Write per-item TFA as competence plus a reference-predictability nuisance (how easy this particular gold is to reproduce, the same for every model) plus a style offset.

How the nuisance is measured. Take the model × item grid of per-item TFA (the 5-model Qwen ladder) and subtract the per-model mean (each model minus its own average), so only item-to-item variation is left. The share of that variation which is identical across all models (the item main effect, a one-way ANOVA on the reference) is the nuisance: 89-96% on every dataset. The other 4-11% is all that remains for competence. Reproducible via scripts/variance_decomp.py.

Because it is the same for every model, the nuisance cancels when you average over items (ranking works), but buries the competence signal within a single item (grading fails).

This predicts no reweighting of TFA can recover the signal. So we tried them all.
Q2 · what we tried · the fixes

Seven cheap fixes, each removing one nuisance

If the per-item quality signal is merely buried under the reference nuisance, then reweighting or contrasting TFA should dig it out. Each fix targets one coordinate of that nuisance.

content-token TFA — mask formatting and LaTeX glue; score only content tokens.

IDF-weighted TFA — up-weight corpus-rare gold tokens, down-weight boilerplate.

surprisal-weighted TFA — up-weight surprising, non-formulaic gold tokens.

TFA-logprob / BPC — a soft gold-token log-probability instead of hard argmax match.

step-shuffle contrast — TFA(gold) minus TFA(gold with its reasoning lines reordered).

answer-swap contrast — TFA(gold) minus TFA(gold with a wrong final answer).

multi-reference TFA — the max TFA over several verified gold solutions.

Each peels off one coordinate: glue, frequency, style, path order, or length.

If the signal were only masked, one of these should uncover it.
Q2 · what we tried · the results

Every cheap fix fails

We ran all seven. None recovers a per-item quality signal: the correlations cluster at zero, and the reweighting variants come out slightly negative (the surprising, hard-to-predict tokens are exactly the ones good models also miss). Structurally, each fix strips just one coordinate of the nuisance and the leftover is still nuisance, not competence, the signature of a signal that is absent, not merely masked.

One cautionary tale. The answer-swap contrast first looked like a real win at +0.35. It was a length artifact: because the corruption changed only the final-answer token, the score collapsed to “predicts the right answer, divided by solution length.” Controlling for length dropped it to zero and we retracted it, now a standing rule: no item-level win is believed until it survives length and difficulty controls.

The signal is absent, not masked. TFA cannot grade an individual solution.
Q3 · a signal that does grade

Rollout process value grades solutions, at a cost

+0.43process value vs judge
+0.19sound vs lucky correct
~100×the cost of TFA

Stop anchoring on a gold trace, measure the model's own reasoning: truncate a solution, let a fixed completer finish it, and score whether it still reaches the right answer. This grades where TFA cannot, even separating sound from lucky correct answers, but only at a mid-strength completer and at ~100x the cost.

A soft verifier, not a cheap judge. The open problem is a cheap, reference-free version.
Conclusions

TL;DR and what is new

The one idea

TFA measures agreement with the reference's style, not reasoning quality, and everything follows.

  • Model ranker: excellent within a family and on hard references; noisy on code; inverts on saturated data; holds across judges.
  • Per-solution grader: essentially fails (≈0 on MATH); no variant fixes it.
  • Rollout process value does grade, weakly, at ~100× the cost.
  • The boundary reaches agents (SWE-bench, tool-calls).

Our unique contributions

  1. First test of TFA's grading claim (prior work assumed it) — it fails.
  2. The mechanism: the 89-96% nuisance decomposition explaining ranking-works / grading-fails.
  3. The boundary map across families, judges, and datasets, including the GSM8K sign-flip.
  4. Reconciliation of the original 0.66 as a metric-and-model-set effect.
  5. Extension to agents: the same within/cross-family boundary on code patches and tool calls.
Path forward · proposal to Sanmi

Where judge-free evaluation goes next

Directions to choose between

  • LLMs vs agents: deepen the math/code boundary, or push into open-ended agents.
  • TFA alternatives: multi-reference (outcome-gated), self-consistency-anchored, per-step signals.
  • The positive bet: reference-free process value grounded in an environment's own success oracle, where no gold trace exists.
Hard constraint. Frontier API models expose no token log-probabilities, so TFA (any teacher-forcing signal) cannot run on them, only open weights. This caps TFA's reach and pushes toward output-only and process-based signals.

Deep-research the scalable-oversight toolkit

The setting is weak-to-strong supervision: overseeing models whose outputs we cannot fully verify.

  • Weak-to-strong supervision
  • Debate and comparative judging
  • Process rewards / rollout value (Math-Shepherd, OmegaPRM), audited for reward hacking
  • Consistency-vs-truth guardrails throughout
Our result is the map: a reference-anchored cheap signal is safe only within a family; elsewhere it rewards style. For frontier-API and agentic settings, go output-grounded and reference-free.
Research agenda · the gap

Scalable oversight is measured at the wrong point

Today an overseer is judged by its accuracy at parity and its cost. But what predicts whether a method scales is the degradation curve: how reliability changes as the solver grows more capable and as it is optimized against the overseer.

  • The current protocol benchmark (Agent Score Difference) explicitly does not test long-horizon capability gaps or optimization pressure over time.
  • Judges are provably hackable: a lone “:” draws false positives from GPT-4o up to 35% of the time, and strong judges are near-random on JudgeBench objective-correctness pairs.
  • Reference-free reward signals get gamed under self-play.
The missing third axis: robustness under capability gap × optimization pressure.
Research agenda · the questions

Four questions, ranked by impact

RQ1 · flagship

Oversight robustness curves. Chart overseer reliability vs solver capability and vs optimization pressure, across math, code, agentic, and subjective domains, and predict the slope from our style/nuisance offset. Turns “oversight breaks at large gaps” into a predictor.

RQ2

Certify an evaluator without full ground truth. A judge nuisance fraction (quality vs surface: verbosity, style, position), anchored on human grades; flags the hackable failures before deployment.

RQ3

Reference-free process signals for agents that survive optimization. Our rollout process value, grounded in the environment oracle, hardened against reward hacking.

RQ4

Does verification beat generation for grading quality? Our item-level null says: not for quality, only for correctness. The backbone under RQ1 and RQ2.

Every cheap evaluator, TFA and LLM judges alike, mixes a quality signal with a surface nuisance.
Research agenda · the bet

Flagship: oversight robustness curves

The impactful-paper template, borrowed from generative modeling: introduce a genuine new axis to a problem treated as two-dimensional, then validate it across modalities with scaling curves. Our new axis is oversight robustness; our modalities are math, code, agentic, and subjective tasks.

What is uniquely ours: not just the benchmark, but a mechanism that predicts the curve. As the solver diverges in style and distribution from the overseer, the nuisance term grows and reliability bends, exactly the offset we measured for TFA.

Respects the frontier constraint. API models expose no token log-probabilities, so the practical toolkit is certified judges (RQ2) + reference-free process signals (RQ3), with TFA the foundation that maps the limits.
Proposal to Sanmi: RQ1 as the flagship, RQ2 as its certification engine, RQ3 as the agentic follow-on.
Appendix · robustness to the judge

Not one judge's opinion

0.75-0.94inter-judge agreement (ρ)
2 familiesgpt-5.2 & Opus 4.8

The model-ranking story above is judge-free (TFA vs accuracy). The item-level results in Part 2 are the only judge-defined ones, so we re-graded the three anchor datasets with a second frontier judge from a different family (Claude Opus 4.8), same rubric. Same pattern: the MATH null stays null and the small GSM8K and Putnam signals replicate, with CIs still excluding zero.

The conclusions are properties of TFA, not of the particular judge we appointed as ground truth.
